title: kuhn
text: On Thomas Kuhn, little treat culture, and gaps in the in between.
What could be more radical than heaven?

Thomas Kuhn, in "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" (1962), uses the "incommensurability of competing paradigms" to describe the axiomatic tension within which our lives on Earth play out. He writes: "in a sense that I am unable to explicate further, the proponents of competing paradigms practice their trades in different worlds... it is why, before they can hope to communicate fully, one group or the other must experience the conversion that we have been calling a paradigm shift. Just because it is a transition between incommensurables, the transition between competing paradigms cannot be made a step at a time, forced by logic and neutral experience. Like the gestalt switch, it must occur all at once (though not necessarily in an instant) or not at all. How, then, are scientists brought to make this transposition? Part of the answer is that they are very often not." Is it then futile to campaign, critique, and care about the state of The System? Is it then foolish to fuel our politics with a belief that our hermeneutical injustices will be eliminated in due time by… humans? Really? To expect that one day, the species which created the means for its own obliteration by choice, will be the same one that will correct these fundamental gaps in due time, seems to me, depending on the weather outside, either an act of faith or a category error.

These days, as late stage capitalism pervades our imaginations of the future and our spiritual thirst is converted into consumer preference, little treat culture tides us over. Our dissatisfactions are efficiently metabolized by The System, which returns various abstractions of "purpose" to us: priced, packaged, and with free next-day shipping (given you've already paid for Prime).

Listen: I'm not saying "don't get that biweekly Molly tea delivered over the 17", as much as I think that is depressingly indicative of our times. I'm not above any of this, and I'm not even critical of it most days. But perhaps the small grace that is that Peach Oolong Milk Tea can fuel the idea that life is indeed worth living - that the kingdom of God is here and now even as we occupy the in between.

Jonathan Lear defines radical hope as hope that "is directed toward a future goodness that transcends the current ability to understand what it is. Radical hope anticipates a good for which those who have the hope as yet lack the appropriate concepts with which to understand it." Optimism has a plan. Radical hope flings the front door open and struts out — walking into the world without particular direction but with particular purpose. When a hermeneutical gap makes a guest appearance in your life, can you resist waltzing through and filling it with whatever vocabulary is at hand? Instead unravel a blanket, unpack a sandwich, and picnic with it. The sun is beating down, and you forgot to put sunscreen on; despite this, can you sit, cross-legged, patiently listening to the wind, with no agenda — because we were always meant to be in the in between, the already but not yet?
Malcolm Guite, "O Sapientia":
I cannot think unless I have been thought,
Nor can I speak unless I have been spoken.
I cannot teach except as I am taught,
Or break the bread except as I am broken.
O Mind behind the mind through which I seek,
O Light within the light by which I see,
O Word beneath the words with which I speak,
O founding, unfound Wisdom, finding me,
O sounding Song whose depth is sounding me,
O Memory of time, reminding me,
My Ground of Being, always grounding me,
My Maker's Bounding Line, defining me,
Come, hidden Wisdom, come with all you bring,
Come to me now, disguised as everything.
Let us consume, slowly, receptively, and with gratitude that begets radical hope. Amen.
